hints: Focus on what allows a mixture of two optical isomers, think about which carbon must have four different groups attached.
Check each chloroalkane for a chiral centre, this quickly rules out two of the structures which have two identical groups on the C-Cl carbon.
For the remaining chiral molecules, count elimination products carefully and remember that pent-2-ene can show E/Z isomerism while more branched alkenes often cannot.
walkthrough:
**Use optical isomerism to find chiral molecules**

A mixture of two optical isomers means the molecule is chiral. It must contain a carbon attached to four different groups.

Condition for chiral centre:
$$\text{chiral C has 4 different substituents}$$

**Rule out achiral options**

Option A is $(CH_3CH_2)_2CHCl$, or 3-chloropentane. The C-Cl carbon has H, Cl and two identical $CH_3CH_2$ groups, so it is achiral.

Option C is $CH_3CH_2CCl(CH_3)_2$, or 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. The C-Cl carbon has two identical $CH_3$ groups, so it is also achiral.

**Apply elimination in ethanolic NaOH**

Heating with NaOH in ethanol causes dehydrohalogenation, removal of $HCl$ from adjacent carbons to form $C=C$.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CHCl-R'} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CH=CH-R'} + \text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Count alkenes including E/Z isomerism**

Option B is $CH_3CH_2CH_2CHClCH_3$, 2-chloropentane. Loss of H from C1 gives pent-1-ene (1 alkene). Loss of H from C3 gives pent-2-ene, which exists as E and Z forms. That is $1 + 2 = 3$ alkenes in total.

Option D is $(CH_3)_2CHCHClCH_3$, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. It is chiral at the C-Cl carbon. Loss of H from C1 gives $CH_2=CHCH(CH_3)_2$, 3-methylbut-1-ene (1 alkene). Loss of H from C3 gives $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3$, 2-methylbut-2-ene. This second alkene has two identical $CH_3$ groups on one $C=C$ carbon, so no E/Z isomerism. That is $1 + 1 = 2$ alkenes in total, which fits the question.

options.A: Incorrect. (CH3CH2)2CHCl is 3-chloropentane. The carbon bearing Cl is bonded to two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral and cannot exist as optical isomers.
options.B: Incorrect. CH3CH2CH2CHClCH3 is 2-chloropentane and is chiral, so it fits the optical isomer part. However elimination gives three alkenes, not two: pent-1-ene plus E-pent-2-ene and Z-pent-2-ene.
options.C: Incorrect. CH3CH2CCl(CH3)2 is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, a tertiary chloroalkane. The C-Cl carbon has two identical methyl groups, so it is achiral and cannot show optical isomerism.
options.D: Correct. (CH3)2CHCHClCH3 is 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. The C-Cl carbon has H, Cl, CH3 and CH(CH3)2, four different groups, so it is chiral. Elimination gives only two alkenes: 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene, with no E/Z duplication for the second product.
